conclusion.strategy_evolution: Pipelining is a dead end; the next probe isolates the streaming floor (pure copy) and DMA-organization parameters (tile size, grid, alignment hints) before another round.

plan.hypothesis: The residual 16-bit streaming gap is per-tile transfer/handshake overhead rather than pipeline depth; a 32KB tile should lift timing-7 from 23.5us toward 22.3us and timing-3 from 21.2us toward 20.3us.

expected_effect.mechanism: Doubling the 16-bit tile to 32KB per GM<->UB burst and per program iteration reduces per-tile instruction and handshake overhead; device-side probe measured bf16 4096x4096 at 23.09us with BLOCK=16384 versus 24.32us with BLOCK=8192 (same protocol, host floor 11.35us).

conclusion.root_cause: The 16-bit tile change works as intended (about 1us on each large 16-bit case) but is smaller than the run-to-run measurement drift of the shared device, and 9 of 12 timing workloads are pinned at a ~13.5us host/launch floor where the candidate already sits within 0.3-0.6us of the reference.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Both targeted predictions held at the workload level: timing-7 bf16 4096x4096 fell from 23.492us to 22.494us (speedup 0.8113 -> 0.8549) and timing-3 fp16 from 21.240us to 20.334us (1.4794 -> 1.5512); timing-6 bf16 1M also improved 14.624 -> 13.372us. conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-apply the 16-bit BLOCK=16384 tile (device-verified win on the three 16-bit timing cases) together with a slimmer host launch path, and stop chasing sub-microsecond host-floor effects afterwards.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Device-level microbenchmarks must use the raw launcher; with it, the bf16 4096x4096 streaming floor is a pure copy at 15.3us versus 23.8us with the 2-add rounding, and each extra FP32 vector pass costs about 4us, which is why op count matters more than tile size on the 16-bit path.

plan.code_changes: Added _round_pipe, an otherwise identical copy of _round_stream whose full-tile loop uses tl.range(..., num_stages=2) so the next GM->UB load overlaps the current tile's convert+2-add+store. _build selects _round_pipe for float16/bfloat16 and keeps the single-stage _round_stream for float32 (a 2-stage fp32 path would need about 192KB UB). plan.hypothesis: The 16-bit streaming path is limited by a single-stage loop with no load/compute overlap (bf16 at ~34.9GB/s vs reference ~43.0GB/s per core); pipelining two stages should recover most of that gap without touching arithmetic or partition style.

expected_effect.mechanism: Overlapping the 16KB next-tile DMA with vector work raises effective GM->UB rate toward the reference's ~43GB/s per core; timing-7 bf16 4096x4096 should fall from 23.5us toward ~20.5us and timing-3 fp16 from 21.2us toward ~19us.

conclusion.root_cause: The 16-bit streaming loop is not limited by load/compute overlap: adding a second pipeline stage materialized no gain, and the residual bf16 4096x4096 gap (23.5us vs reference 19.3us) must come from DMA burst organization, per-core concurrency, or the dtype conversion path rather than from pipeline depth.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Two-stage pipelining produced no measurable change on the workloads it targeted: timing-3 fp16 4096x4096 21.258us vs 21.240us in round 2, timing-7 bf16 4096x4096 23.566us vs 23.492us, timing-11 fp32 105.7us vs 106.3us (fp32 was deliberately left single-stage). conclusion.next_suggestion: Revert to the single-stage kernel (round 2). conclusion.debug_lesson: num_stages on tl.range neither helped nor hurt on this backend for this kernel; the JIT-vs-raw-launcher distinction (60us vs 13.4us host cost) must be respected when designing any device-time microbenchmark.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Pipelining is a dead end; the next probe isolates the streaming floor (pure copy) and DMA-organization parameters (tile size, grid, alignment hints) before another round.
